clauses.reason: Executive Order 6526 of December 21, 1933 states: "do order that the application for exemption by the Southern Plow Manufacturers Association, be and is hereby denied". A denial of an application for exemption from a code commands nothing after it issues: its command was performed and exhausted on December 21, 1933, the date the order was signed, and the order states no later effective date. The applicant's continuing obligation after the denial is the code's own operation, which the order approving the Farm Equipment Code governs and which ended with the repeal; it is not a surviving command of the denial. The Administrator's report of November 21, 1933 that the order adopts is a recital, not a deadline or a command. The later event is the repeal on June 14, 1935: section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". Schechter (295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date.

Executive Order 6526 of December 21, 1933 states: "but that the words \"members of the Association\" in the last sentence of Article VI, Section 2, be and is hereby changed to \"employers who have agreed to the Code.\"" That command changes the text of the Code of Fair Competition for the Farm Equipment Industry (approved by EO 6307, a held order) under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and it has legal effect only as a term of the approved code: under section 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, and under sections 3(c) and 3(f) violations were restrainable in equity and punishable as misdemeanors. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides: "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no other effective date, so the wording change ended as a prospective operative command on June 14, 1935. No earlier end is shown: no held text other than EO 6307 and this order names the Farm Equipment Code, and none cancels, suspends or supersedes it. The June 16, 1935 expiry is not an end because section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936. Schechter (295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date.

inventory_overrides.reason: The machine inventory treats the whole operative paragraph as one clause, but it holds two separate commands: the denial of the application for exemption (exhausted when signed) and the change of wording in the code (a modification that lasts as long as the code approval). The corrected inventory separates them; this clause is the denial, including the authority sentence that introduces it.
Second command of the paragraph: the change of two quoted phrases in Article VI, Section 2 of the code, separated from the denial because its end is the repeal, not performance on signing.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6526 (December 21, 1933) decides an application under the Farm Equipment Code: it denies the Southern Plow Manufacturers Association's application for exemption and changes one phrase in Article VI, Section 2 of the code. The denial is exhausted by performance on its date and the wording change is a modification of the code's text that operates only through the section 3 approval, so it ended with the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I on June 14, 1935 (S.J. Res. 113 section 2). Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); applies SHARED_ANALYSIS.md, including its rule for denials of exemption.

No held record shows the code cancelled, suspended, superseded or revoked before June 14, 1935. The denial is exhausted on its date under the shared analysis, with the June 14, 1935 repeal as a later event; the wording change ended with the repeal. June 16, 1935 is not an end, because section 1 of S.J. Res. 113 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date.","independent_command_check":"No appointment, delegation, direction to a government agency or other command independent of the code appears. The report of November 21, 1933 that the order \"adopted and approved\" is an input to the decision, not a direction to report, and the machine's report-deadline label for it does not describe a command. The denial is the one-time determination covered by the shared analysis; the wording change is code-dependent.","savings_check":"Read S.J. No held source continues this approval, a prosecution under it or any command of this order after June 14, 1935; accrued acts, liabilities and the section 5 exemption for completed action are recorded as transferred or accrued and not as continued operation.","scope_check":"Two operative commands, separated by the inventory correction: (1) the denial of the Southern Plow Manufacturers Association's application for exemption from the minimum wage in the code, and (2) the change of the words \"members of the Association\" to \"employers who have agreed to the Code\" in Article VI, Section 2. The order says no case of injustice was made out \"respecting minimum rates\" and that the wording is \"unnecessarily restrictive\"; those are findings. The order's own title (APP page record) also names the Blount Plow Works, but the held text decides only the Association's application and the wording change, and I do not read a separate command about the Blount Plow Works into it. savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1935-05-27: date the section 3 delegation was declared unconstitutional; validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not an end date
source_notes.reason: Schechter, 295 U.S. 495, held the code provisions in question invalid on both of its grounds; recorded as a validity characterization of section 3 code approvals, not as an end date for this order. It adjudicated the Live Poultry Code provisions and cancelled or withdrew no other approving order.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1933-06-16: date the Act was approved; states the repealed legal effects of a code approval, not an end date
source_notes.reason: Sections 3(a)-(f) state the legal effects of an approved code that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed: the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition (3(b)), district courts could restrain violations (3(c)), and violations were misdemeanors (3(f)).
